claims.text: AlCrFeCoNi HEA naturally forms a passive oxide film.
The coupled tribo-corrosion behavior of AlCrFeCoNi is predominantly governed by competition between mechanical passive-film removal and electrochemical film regeneration.
Mechanical sliding can remove the passive film faster than it reforms.
Removal of the passive film exposes bare metal and accelerates local corrosion.
Accelerated local corrosion further destabilizes the passive oxide layer.
Passive-film integrity, thickness, and renewal dynamics dictate local degradation behavior.
Varying sliding speed and normal load changes the rate of passive-film removal.
Operating just below the pitting potential can be used to probe passive-film reformation kinetics.
Combined tribo-corrosion produces degradation greater than the additive contributions of isolated wear and corrosion.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce greater total degradation than corrosion-only exposure.
Loss of the protective passive film will enhance wear rates.
Corrosion current density will be higher in actively worn regions.
Synergistic degradation will be strongest when passive-film removal is faster than electrochemical repassivation.
Lower loads can reduce synergy by permitting passive-film recovery between sliding events.
Electrolyte conditions that accelerate repassivation can reduce the tribo-corrosion synergy.
Electrolyte pH alteration can increase repassivation sufficiently to minimize synergistic degradation.
In-situ Raman spectroscopy or XPS can continuously monitor oxide-film thickness and composition during sliding.
A lack of correlation between film loss and corrosion, together with no degradation beyond the sum of isolated wear and corrosion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
